title: Nikesh Arora's Palo Alto Networks Hit an All-Time High. His Bet: AI Makes Hackers Worse, Not Cybersecurity Obsolete.
excerpt: The Indian-born CEO used Anthropic's frontier model to find five years of vulnerabilities in six weeks. His $240 billion company has doubled while the market panicked over software's future.
body:
Nikesh Arora has a message for anyone who thinks artificial intelligence will kill the cybersecurity industry: you are confused, and his stock price agrees.

Palo Alto Networks, the $240 billion cybersecurity giant led by the Indian-born CEO, hit a new 52-week high this week at $306, capping a remarkable recovery from the panic that gripped software stocks earlier this year. While the rest of the software world worried that AI would make their products obsolete, Arora quietly doubled his company's share price — and spent $10 million of his own money buying the dip along the way.

## The Vulnerability Machine

The latest catalyst came this week, when Arora revealed on the *Twenty Minute VC* podcast that Palo Alto had used Mythos — Anthropic's frontier AI model that was deemed too powerful for unrestricted release — to discover five years' worth of software vulnerabilities in just six weeks. The demonstration was not an academic exercise. It was proof of concept for Arora's central thesis: that AI dramatically expands the attack surface, and the companies best positioned to exploit AI for defence will see demand surge, not collapse.

"I'm still confused why the market is treating AI as a threat" to cybersecurity, Arora told analysts during the company's fiscal third-quarter earnings call in early June. The numbers backed him up. Revenue rose to $3 billion for the quarter, up from $2.6 billion a year earlier, and the company raised its full-year outlook. More than 110 enterprise customers completed what Palo Alto calls "platformizations" during the quarter — consolidating fragmented cybersecurity tools onto Palo Alto's unified platform.

## The Platform Play

Arora's strategy rests on a bet that enterprises drowning in point-solution cybersecurity products will consolidate. A typical large company might run forty or fifty separate security tools from different vendors — firewalls from one, endpoint detection from another, cloud security from a third. Palo Alto's pitch: collapse them all into one platform, and use AI to correlate threats across the entire stack.

The market was initially sceptical. When Arora announced the platformization strategy in February 2024, the stock dropped. Two years later, the results are hard to argue with. Customers who platformize spend more, renew at higher rates, and give Palo Alto visibility into threats that fragmented competitors simply cannot match.

"To the extent we are creating proprietary data in security, that is not going to be replaced by an LLM," Arora said. The argument is compelling: Palo Alto sees real-world threat data from thousands of enterprises, and that proprietary corpus — not publicly available training data — is what makes its AI models useful. An AI without threat intelligence is just a very fast guesser.

## The Diaspora Angle

Arora's career arc is a case study in the Indian-origin tech leader's playbook — one that increasingly runs through cybersecurity. Born in Uttar Pradesh, educated at IIT Varanasi and Northeastern University, he spent 10 years at Google as Chief Business Officer (reporting directly to Larry Page) before a high-profile stint as president of SoftBank. He took the Palo Alto Networks CEO role in 2018 and has since built it into the world's most valuable pure-play cybersecurity company.

For Indian tech professionals in the US — particularly those at enterprises now under pressure to upgrade their security posture against AI-powered threats — Arora's ascent matters. Cybersecurity is one of the fastest-growing segments in enterprise technology, projected to reach $300 billion globally by 2028. It is also one of the few sectors where AI is an unambiguous tailwind, not a headwind that threatens jobs.

Around 1,000 companies reached out to Palo Alto over the past two months, Arora disclosed, "to talk about their cyber posture, cyber infrastructure, and how we can help them get through this period of living the future with frontier AI models being cyber-capable." The development of models like Anthropic's Claude Mythos — powerful enough that Anthropic offered early access to cyber defenders before general release — has made the conversation urgent.

For once, the cybersecurity industry's perennial message of fear is also its growth story. Nikesh Arora just happens to be the one selling both.
